summary: Recommends that IPv6 forwarding must handle prefixes of any length from 0 to 128 and not assume particular lengths, even though subnets using SLAAC are normally 64 bits long.

eli5.summary: Mail sorters should read the whole address, not assume every street is the same length.

questions: does ipv6 routing support any prefix length
does ipv6 forwarding support any prefix length
what is longest match first in ipv6
is ipv6 limited to 64 bit prefixes
subtitle: Routers should forward IPv6 on any prefix length from 0 to 128, not just the familiar /64.

tldr.problem: Because IPv6 subnets using SLAAC conventionally use a /64 prefix, some people wrongly believe IPv6 prefixes can only be /127 or any length up to /64, and forwarding gear might be built around that belief.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires forwarding to follow longest-match-first on prefixes of any length up to /128, in steps of 1, with no restriction on prefix length built into the design.
tldr.outcome: Prefix length limits can still be set by deployment-specific policy, but never by the design of the forwarding process itself.

today: RFC 7608 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 198, July 2015). The metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why a Recommendation Was Needed
sections.content:
Discussions of the 64-bit boundary in IPv6 addressing (RFC 7421) showed a need for a clear statement of which bits forwarding decisions may use. That document could not provide it, because it was out of scope.

The prefix length is a parameter used in IPv6 routing and forwarding, as in IPv4, under the Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR) architecture. It can be any number from zero to 128.
sections.eli5: Some people thought every IPv6 street had to be the same length. This document says that is not so, and the mail sorter must cope with any length.

sections.title: The 64-Bit Boundary and the Misunderstanding
sections.content:
RFC 4291 says IPv6 unicast addresses are aggregatable with prefixes of arbitrary bit-length, similar to IPv4 under CIDR (RFC 4632). Yet there is a persistent misreading that prefixes can be either /127 (RFC 6164) or any length up to /64. The RFC says this is mainly induced by the 64-bit boundary.

Quoting RFC 7421, the RFC notes that the /64 boundary was introduced after the initial design of IPv6, when /80 had been expected. That history, plus the later addition of /127 prefixes for point-to-point links, shows the intent that this part of the architecture could change when justified.

The RFC states it is fundamental not to tie routing and forwarding to the semantics of the IPv6 prefix or address.
sections.eli5: The rule that streets are 64 steps long was added late, and it used to be planned as 80. Since it changed once, nobody should build machines that can only handle one length.

sections.title: Longest-Match-First
sections.content:
Forwarding relies on the longest-match-first algorithm. If the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) holds two prefixes of different lengths that both match the destination address bit for bit up to their own lengths, the longer prefix is used.

The RFC says IPv6 forwarding must follow this rule regardless of prefix length, unless some overriding policy is configured.

This does not conflict with the 64-bit boundary used by some schemes based on stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC), such as the Ethernet scheme in RFC 2464. RFC 7421 clarifies that /64 is just one parameter of the SLAAC process, and longer prefix lengths are in operational use, whether manually configured or based on DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: If two signposts both fit your address, follow the one that matches more of it. That works no matter how long the signposts are.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The requirements are short. IPv6 implementations MUST conform to the rules in Section 5.1 of RFC 4632.

Decision-making processes for forwarding MUST NOT restrict the length of IPv6 prefixes by design. In particular, forwarding processes MUST be designed to process prefixes of any length up to /128, by increments of 1.

Policies may still limit the prefix lengths advertised within a domain or on an interconnection link. The RFC says such policies are deployment specific or driven by administrative considerations, not by the forwarding design.
sections.eli5: The machine must be able to handle every length. A network owner can still choose to allow only some lengths, but that is their choice, not a limit built into the machine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document says it introduces no security issues beyond those discussed in RFC 4291. It points to RFC 4942 and an Internet-Draft on operational security for IPv6 networks for wider IPv6 security discussion.
sections.eli5: Letting the sorter read every address length does not open any new doors for troublemakers.
